What the check is meant to establish

children.label: What the check is meant to establish

children.value: The latent-state agent is a low-dimensional description of behaviour. Its six parameters are meant to capture informative and interpretable tendencies of each participant, such as how concentrated the nets are, how quickly a change of the latent state is adopted, how strongly the colour cue is used, and how variable the placements are, and to order participants reliably along these dimensions, so that the parameters can be related to questionnaire scores. The model is not meant to reproduce every placement of a participant, and no model of this size can. The parameters are estimated from 54 summary features of a session by simulation-based inference (
), so that the relevant standard is how well the model reproduces these behavioural summaries, at the level at which they are used.
Three questions follow from this use of the model:
Where the fitted model predicts a different value than observed, is the deviation small relative to the differences between participants?
Does the fitted model reproduce the ordering of participants on each feature, and how close does it come to the agreement that would be expected if the model had generated the data?
Does the reproduction of individual differences hold within each instruction condition?

A frequently used summary, the share of participants whose observed value falls inside the central 95 % interval of their own posterior predictive distribution, answers none of these questions. That interval reflects only the simulation variability of one session at the participant’s posterior. With 171 to 188 trials per session, the summary features are estimated precisely, and the intervals are narrow: for the main features they are 0.6 to 0.8 between-participant standard deviations wide. A small offset that is shared by all participants then places many observed values outside the interval, even when the model reproduces the differences between participants almost perfectly. The share is reported for completeness, but it is not used to judge the model.
For each participant, 100 parameter vectors were drawn from the posterior, and the agent was simulated with each of them on the participant’s own trial schedule (

). The 54 summary features were computed from each simulated session in the same way as from the participant’s session. The analysis includes the 59 participants for whom the latent-state model had the highest posterior probability in the model comparison.

children.value: For the levels of behaviour, the fitted model reproduces both the values and the differences between participants closely. The median offset is 0.30 between-participant SDs, and the median rank correlation reaches 86 % of the agreement expected if the model had generated the data. The features that summarise the spread of the allocation, accuracy and interception, the trial-to-trial change of the placement and the use of the colour cues are reproduced with rank correlations of 0.77 to 0.97, at 87 % to 100 % of the expected agreement (table below). The level features of the response to oddballs are reproduced less well (ratio 0.34 to 0.70).

children.value: The rank correlations within conditions rest on 21 (C1), 25 (C2) and 13 (C3) participants. In C1 and C2 they reach a median of 91 % and 88 % of the expected rank correlation within the same condition (level features). In C3 they reach 63 %, although the expected rank correlation in C3 is as high as in the other conditions (median .90). The smaller between-participant variation in C3 therefore does not explain the lower correlations: with the C3 participants’ own posteriors and schedules, the model would order them as well as in C1 and C2. The difference is largest for the error relative to the hidden-state target (ρ = .55, expected .86), the proportion of large shifts (.46, expected .92), the rate of switches between the two state directions without an event (.52, expected .87) and the learned cue offset (.53, expected .88). With 13 participants each of these correlations is uncertain, but the pattern is consistent over features. It concerns the participants who were told the structure; the differences between them in how often they move their placement by large amounts are captured less well than in C1 and C2.

): participants alternate between precise placements and discrete moves to the other state’s direction or to the location of a preceding oddball, whereas the model represents all off-target placements by a Gaussian shift of the allocation on every trial. The mean variability of the placements is reproduced (

Differences, ratios and slopes, such as the change of the defense rate over the session or the ratio of the shift after oddballs to the shift on regular trials, are reproduced in value (median offset 0.57 SD) but only partly in the ordering of participants (median ρ = 0.27, at 46 % of the expected agreement). These statistics combine two estimates from one session and are less reliable than the levels from which they are formed; the expected rank correlation is correspondingly lower (median 0.70). For five features it is below .60, so that even the data-generating model would order participants on them only weakly:

The excess variability is located in the upper part of the distribution of the placement errors (

; regular trials, 20 posterior draws per participant). The median error of the placement centre relative to the hidden-state target is reproduced (observed minus predicted, median over participants −0.5°), but the 75th and 90th percentiles are 17° and 29° higher in participants than predicted (for 81 % and 93 % of participants), and the share of placements more than 90° from the target is 21 % against 13 %. The same holds for the change of the placement centre from one trial to the next (90th percentile 26° higher). Participants’ errors are thus more often either small or very large (close to the direction of the other latent state, 120° away), whereas the Gaussian placement noise of the model produces intermediate errors. The positive offsets of the mean error (+0.59 SD) and of the within-state variability (+0.69 SD) follow from the same upper tail.
Among the level features, those of the response to oddballs are reproduced least well (ratio 0.34 to 0.70), consistent with the discrete moves to the location of an oddball described above.
Consequences for the use of the parameters

children.label: Consequences for the use of the parameters

children.value: The behavioural dimensions on which the parameters are defined are those on which the model reproduces the ordering of participants closely: the concentration of the allocation (precision weighting), the variability of the placements (placement noise), the learned cue offset (cue sensitivity), and the trial-to-trial change and the switching of the placement (belief momentum and the switch probability). The construct-validity check confirms the corresponding associations between each parameter and its behavioural measure (

). The systematic deviations concern the trial-to-trial variability of the placements and statistics of the response to oddballs. They are reported as a limit of the model: placement noise summarises all placements away from the predicted direction, including discrete moves, and noise reactivity, whose behavioural measure is the response to oddballs, is interpreted with its posterior uncertainty.

Deviations that could be addressed without a new mechanism

children.label: Deviations that could be addressed without a new mechanism

children.value: Two deviations follow from the prior ranges rather than from the mechanism of the model, and could be addressed by widening the range and retraining the posterior network (no new parameter):

The believed cue offset approaches cue sensitivity × 70°, so that offsets above the true 70° cannot be represented. For the 27 participants whose 95 % posterior interval reaches the upper bound of 1, the predicted learned cue offset is about 10° below the observed one (medians 64° to 67° against 73° to 78°, in all three conditions). Widening the prior to, for example, 0 to 1.3 would let the parameter represent an overestimated offset, and would be expected to remove the offset of
(+0.30 SD) and to improve its rank correlation in C3, where 10 of 13 participants are at the bound.

For 11 participants the 95 % interval reaches the bound of 0.873 rad (50°). Their offsets on the variability features are not larger than those of the other participants (for example +0.77 against +0.67 SD for

), so that the bound does not explain the deviations, but their placement noise is estimated with an upper limit, which compresses the differences at the top of the distribution used in the questionnaire analyses (RQ3). A wider range (for example to 1.2 rad) would remove this.

In addition, the five features with an expected rank correlation below .60 could be removed from the feature set at the same retraining, since they add noise to the summary network without information about differences between participants.

The deviations in the variability and upper tail of the placements, in the response to oddballs, and in C3 share one source, discrete moves of the placement to the other state’s direction or to an oddball location. The mechanisms that would reproduce them (allocation centred on a sampled state, following an oddball with a free probability) were examined and not adopted because they reduce the identifiability of the parameters or overlap in meaning with noise reactivity (

The posterior predictive checks motivated the sixth parameter of the agent. The five-parameter agent placed its nets at the predictive mean on every trial and was too stable: for nearly all participants, the features of trial-to-trial change lay above the predictive interval. The excess variability was identified as variability of the placement within a latent state that is not explained by the outcome noise of the task, and
was added as a circular Gaussian shift of the predictive distribution before the nets are allocated (see
). The checks of that development step were computed with an earlier network at N = 34; the chapter of that state is kept in
. The trial-level analysis of October 2026 refines its conclusion: the remaining variability is not only undirected scatter but includes discrete moves to a small number of locations.
